articles.abstract: Marvin L. Birnbaum, MD, PhD passed away in May 2026. He was a pioneer and leader in both Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Disaster Medicine. He was dedicated to developing EMS and Disaster Medicine as professions and academic disciplines. Dr. Birnbaum was Editor-in-Chief of Prehospital and Disaster Medicine (PDM) for 23 years and served terms as the World Association for Disaster and Emergency Medicine (WADEM) President and was a member of the WADEM Board of Directors for 35 Years. This editorial is a tribute to Dr. Birnbaum.

articles.title: Two-dimensional shear wave elastography-based assessment of liver stiffness in critically ill patients with septic shock: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: The acute effects of resuscitation on the liver during septic shock, as assessed through liver stiffness, are not well understood. The objective of this pilot study was to evaluate liver stiffness in patients with septic shock using two-dimensional shear wave elastography (2D-SWE). This prospective study was conducted at a 30-bed ICU of a university hospital. Patients with septic shock, who had apparently normal liver status before current illness, requiring vasopressors for ≥ 24 h were considered within 7 days after the onset of shock. Patients with pre-existing liver diseases, congestive heart failure, intra-abdominal hypertension, recent history of abdominal trauma/surgery, body mass index ≥ 35 kg/m2, and pregnancy were excluded. Liver stiffness was measured by 2D-SWE scan, which was repeated after at least 4 weeks of recovery from shock. Fifty-two patients aged 44 (34-63) years in septic shock with median SOFA score 9 (IQR 6-11) were included. The median liver stiffness after the onset of septic shock was 30 kPa (IQR 25.2-34.2), a significantly higher than normal value (< 7 kPa). This stiffness was significantly associated with vasoactive dose index (VDI) [linear regression coefficient (β): 23.02; 95%CI 16.60-29.69; p = 0.001]. The limited follow-up measurements (in 18 survivors) revealed a marked reduction in liver stiffness values from 29 kPa (IQR 26-32) to 6 kPa (IQR 5.4-6.4). Assessment of liver through 2D-SWE, after the onset of septic shock in apparently normal liver status pre-illness, revealed increased stiffness. However, it reverted to normal once clinical condition improved. Clinical Trials Registry - India: CTRI/2023/06/053891.

articles.title: One-Hour Simulation Curriculum Improves Neonatal Resuscitation Skills of Emergency Medicine Residents.
articles.abstract: To evaluate whether a 1-hour neonatal resuscitation (NR) simulation curriculum improves emergency medicine (EM) resident skills, competency, and level of comfort in NR. NR skills were assessed during a 7-minute simulation conducted before and after a 45-minute educational session. Performance was assessed using the validated Neonatal Resuscitation Performance Evaluation (NRPE) tool. Time to each successful intervention during the simulation was recorded. Residents completed surveys at 3 time points: before the session (pre), immediately after (post), and at the end of the year (post-post). Surveys assessed baseline NR experience, knowledge, and self-reported competency in NR skills. Fourteen third-year EM residents participated. There was a significant median improvement in total NRPE scores and in the subset scores of the bag-mask ventilation, intubation, and chest compressions skills. There was a significant decrease in the median time to obtaining initial heart rate, starting positive pressure ventilation, and to successful intubation. There was no significant difference in the time to initiating chest compressions. All 4 self-reported competency measures showed significant median improvement immediately postintervention. This improvement was maintained for 2 items in the post-post survey. Knowledge assessment scores improved significantly from pre- to postintervention. A 1-hour, NR skill-based simulation curriculum significantly improved NR skills, knowledge, and confidence among senior EM residents. This curriculum could serve as a valuable intervention to address gaps in NR training and can help fulfill proposed Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education requirements.

articles.title: Working through the walls: maintaining emergency department operations during major renovations in a canadian tertiary care centre.
Who works the night shift? Workforce design in emergency medicine.
Deviations From Recommended Drug Dosing in the Prehospital Treatment of Pediatric Patients.
articles.abstract: Pediatric medication safety is a priority area for research and quality improvement in emergency medical services (EMS). While medication errors may occur due to active failures, latent drivers of deviations from recommended dosages (DRD) are incompletely understood. We sought to understand the prevalence of DRDs and the factors associated with them. We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients included in a quality improvement registry for prehospital pediatric medication safety. We included nine EMS agencies with uniform patient care protocols providing 9-1-1 services to the metropolitan area of a midsized city in the U.S. Our primary outcome was the prevalence of DRDs (doses ≥20% above or below protocolized doses). We identified DRDs by checking weight-based doses against weight-based and absolute thresholds. We assessed the prevalence of DRDs by medication, age, clinician impression, and administration route. We assessed associations between these factors and DRDs with logistic regression, then performed adjusted analyses with generalized linear mixed models. We assessed the relationship between weight estimation error and DRDs with a linear mixed model. We explored the potential effect of fixed-dosage formulations, full-vial doses, and volumetric limits of intranasal administration on DRDs. We analyzed 386 medication administrations for 240 patients. The overall prevalence of DRDs was 46.4% (n = 179), and most were underdoses (n = 143, 79.9%). Among common medications, the number and prevalence of DRDs were: ondansetron (n = 29, 85.3%), midazolam (n = 35, 50.0%), fentanyl (n = 55, 45.5%), and epinephrine (n = 26, 44.8%). The DRDs were most common via the intranasal route (n = 62, 69.7%) and among school-aged children (n = 50, 55.6%). Ondansetron (aOR 36.9, 95%CI 6.3-217.6) and the intranasal route (aOR 7.3, 95%CI 2.9-18.6) were associated with higher odds of DRDs. We found no association between weight estimation error and DRDs. Exclusion of potential fixed-dosage formulations and full-vial doses was associated with fewer DRDs (81.6% vs. 42.5%). Only 2% of intranasal fentanyl DRDs could be explained by volumetric limits. We observed DRDs to be common in the prehospital treatment of children, and they varied by medication and route. Possible latent sources of error include protocol design, medication formularies, and heuristics. The clinical significance of DRDs is uncertain.

articles.title: Adhesive small bowel obstruction in the virgin abdomen: comparable phenotype, divergent management.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: In small bowel obstruction (SBO), the absence of prior abdominal surgery is commonly interpreted as a marker of higher-risk pathology and is often associated with a lower threshold for early operative intervention. Whether this assumption reflects differences in disease phenotype or decision-making remains uncertain. This post hoc analysis of a prospective, multicenter cohort study included consecutive adults with CT-confirmed mechanical SBO. Analyses were restricted to patients with adhesion-related SBO to enable comparison between virgin abdomen adhesive SBO (vaASBO) and prior-surgery adhesive SBO (psASBO). Clinical presentation, imaging findings, management strategies, and 60-day outcomes, including patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), were evaluated. Analyses were associative and unadjusted. Among 1,737 patients, 417 (24.0%) had no prior abdominal surgery; adhesions accounted for 30% of cases in this subgroup. The adhesion-restricted cohort included 982 patients, of whom 127 (12.9%) had vaASBO. Clinical and radiological features were similar between groups; however, management differed substantially. Patients with vaASBO had higher rates of direct-to-surgery (+ 15.0% points), lower use of water-soluble contrast (- 19.1% points), and higher rates of nonoperative management (NOM) failure (+ 25.1% points). Among patients undergoing surgery, complication rates were lower in vaASBO (9.2% vs. 23.3%), with similar rates of major complications, mortality, and length of stay. Among patients successfully managed nonoperatively, clinical outcomes and PROMs were comparable. In an adhesion-restricted cohort, patients with and without prior abdominal surgery had comparable clinical phenotype, yet management diverged. These findings suggest that surgical history is associated with treatment selection beyond measured markers of disease severity. A CT-guided, risk-stratified approach may provide a more consistent and reproducible basis for decision-making and reduce unnecessary surgery without compromising clinical or patient-reported outcomes.

articles.title: Exploring risk groups for concomitant injuries in facial fracture patients: a data-driven analysis.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Patients with facial fractures are a diverse group with varying injury mechanisms and extent of injury. These patients often suffer from concomitant injuries (CIs) of different severity outside the facial region, some of which are life-threatening and may require urgent care. Therefore, early identification of patients at risk for CI is important. This study aimed to investigate exploratory risk groups for concomitant injuries in patients with facial fractures, focusing on the impact of injury energy, sex and age on the prevalence and type of concomitant injury. In this retrospective cohort study, a data-driven analysis was used to perform statistical analysis and identify risk groups for different CIs. The study included 4170 patients with facial fractures evaluated at tertiary trauma centres from January 2013 to October 2020. 70.9% of patients with facial fractures were male. Patients' mean age was 45.7 years. Of the injury mechanisms, 36.0% were classified as high-energy trauma. In all, 31.7% of facial fracture patients had some type of CI. Female patients had more CIs than male patients (34.0% vs. 30.8%). The occurrence of CIs increased progressively with age, peaking in the age group 90-94 years, where over 55% of patients experienced CIs. However, considerable variation was observed in CI types across age groups. Due to the high CI risk in facial fracture patients, in conjunction with assessment and imaging of the facial trauma, we encourage routinely ruling out CIs, with a special focus on high-risk CI groups.

articles.title: Hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide mesh tube versus β-tricalcium phosphate granules in locking plate fixation of proximal humeral fractures: a retrospective comparative study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Proximal humeral fractures in older adults are often accompanied by metaphyseal bone defects, leading to reduction loss after plate fixation. Fibular allograft struts provide effective augmentation. However, their availability is limited. This study aimed to compare the outcomes of using hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide (HA/PLLA) mesh tubes as endosteal struts and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) granules for augmentation in locking plate osteosynthesis for proximal humeral fractures. This retrospective study included 42 adult patients who underwent locking plate fixation for acute, closed proximal humeral fractures at a single institution between 2013 and 2022. Among them, 20 patients received endosteal strut-HA/PLLA mesh tube (group E), and 22 received β-TCP granules (group G). Demographics, radiographic outcomes (humeral head height and neck-shaft angle), range of motion, complications, and surgical parameters were compared between the two groups. Group E showed a significantly smaller mean change in humeral head height than group G (1.5 ± 3.1 vs. 4.0 ± 4.0 mm, p = 0.01). No significant difference in the mean change in neck-shaft angle was observed between the two groups (p = 0.31). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed in shoulder range of motion, complication rates, operative time, or blood loss between the two groups. The use of HA/PLLA mesh tube as an intramedullary strut in locking plate osteosynthesis provided superior maintenance of humeral head height compared with β-TCP granules, without increasing complications. Endosteal strut-HA/PLLA mesh tubes may be a practical and safe alternative to allograft struts for augmentation in settings where allografts are unavailable.

articles.title: Interobserver Agreement in Pediatric Asthma Examination Findings Between Emergency Medical Services and Emergency Department Clinicians.
articles.abstract: Asthma exacerbations constitute 10-15% of all pediatric emergency medical services (EMS) calls. There are several validated scoring tools to assess acute asthma severity, which have good inter-rater reliability and correlate with clinical outcomes in the emergency department (ED), but have not been validated with EMS clinicians. This study sought to assess the level of agreement between EMS and ED clinicians on components of asthma scoring tools to inform a prehospital asthma severity scoring tool. We conducted a prospective observational study of children 2-18 years old transported by EMS with an impression of asthma exacerbation to five pediatric EDs. EMS and ED clinicians independently completed surveys assessing the patient's exam on arrival to the ED. Survey items were drawn from existing asthma scoring tools and refined by focus groups and a Delphi process with EMS clinicians and expert stakeholders. To determine agreement between EMS and ED clinicians regarding survey items, inter-rater reliability was calculated using Kappa and intraclass correlation coefficient for binary and ordinal variables, respectively. We enrolled a convenience sample of 295 children with a median age of 7 years (inter-quartile range 3-12 years). There was slight agreement among EMS and ED clinicians (κ = 0.01-0.20) for suprasternal retractions and fair agreement (κ = 0.21-0.40) for tachypnea, accessory muscle use, and elevated respiratory rate. There was poor agreement (ICC = 0-0.50) for breathlessness, work of breathing, degree of hypoxia, type of wheeze, and wheezing intensity. We observed limited agreement between EMS and ED clinicians when assessing children for components of asthma severity scores. Developing a prehospital asthma exacerbation severity scoring tool to guide EMS interventions may be challenging. Further research is needed to determine whether education improves EMS performance with asthma scoring tools or whether standardized EMS asthma protocols, regardless of exacerbation severity, improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Access to supervised consumption services in the emergency department: patient characteristics and outcomes.
articles.abstract: Supervised consumption services have rarely been integrated into hospital environments. This study aimed to describe the characteristics of the first 50 emergency department (ED) patients who accessed a hospital-based supervised consumption service. A secondary goal was to evaluate any adverse events. This study was carried out in a large urban acute care emergency department. Using a standardized data abstraction template, characteristics of the patient, emergency department visit, and supervised consumption visit were independently extracted by two reviewers from the patient's chart and electronic health record. Descriptive statistics are shown. The first 50 emergency department patients to access the hospital-based supervised consumption service made a total of 66 visits between October 3, 2019, and September 10, 2020. Most were male (31, 62%) and were sleeping in shelters or outside (30, 60%); 15 (30%) were prescribed opioid agonist treatment in the community. Hospital admission was necessary for 19 patients (38%). Adverse events were infrequent. Emergency department patients are open to using supervised consumption services. Further research is needed to explore how access to supervised substance use in the emergency department influences patient and staff safety.

articles.title: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Quality During the Transition in Care from Paramedic Services to Emergency Department Teams.
articles.abstract: In patients who experience out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), high quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is associated with improved outcomes. The transition of care from paramedic services to emergency department (ED) teams represents a potentially vulnerable period where CPR quality may deteriorate. This study evaluated CPR quality during the prehospital-to-ED transition. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA transported to a tertiary academic ED between August 2023 and August 2024. Metrics assessing CPR quality were obtained from prehospital and ED defibrillator recordings. Four predefined intervals were analyzed: paramedic baseline, paramedic pre-transition, ED post-transition, and ED baseline. The primary outcome was each adherence to the American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines defined as the mean depth of compressions, mean rate of compressions, and mean chest compression fraction for each interval. Secondary outcomes included comparison between intervals for each metric. Continuous variables were compared using a linear mixed effect model and comparison of categorical data, including the proportion of cases adhering to AHA guidelines, was done using the Cochran's Q test. Thirty-five OHCA cases met inclusion criteria. Mean patient age was 49.9 years (SD 13.6), and 80.0% were male. Mean CCF was guideline compliant throughout all intervals (89-92%) with no significant differences between intervals. Compression rate was guideline compliant across all intervals (109.9-117.5 compressions/minute). Compression depth was guideline compliant during paramedic intervals (5.8 and 5.9 cm) and was significantly higher (p < 0.001) during ED transition and ED baseline intervals (6.4 and 6.8 cm) exceeding guideline targets. No significant differences across intervals were observed in the proportion of cases meeting guideline targets for CCF, rate, or depth. Quality of CPR was overall maintained during the transition of care from paramedic services to the ED, with no deterioration in chest compression fraction or overall guideline adherence. Compression depth exceeded guideline recommendations in the ED, representing a potential target for future quality improvement initiatives.
